extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in media and communication studies (upper-level undergraduates, graduate students, and instructors)
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and criteria for analyzing how ideology shapes media content, including theoretical definitions, levels of influence, mechanisms (ownership, sources, routines), and empirical techniques for detecting ideological effects in news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideology as a 'relatively-formal and articulated-system of meanings, values and beliefs' (Williams) and as 'an integrated set of frames of reference through which each of us sees the world' (Becker).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideology governs perception of the world and controls what is seen as 'natural' or 'obvious.' Use these conceptions to identify the coherent worldview reflected in media messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideology as social integration mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideology functions as a symbolic mechanism that serves as a cohesive and integrating force in society, enabling diverse social strata to make compatible responses to changing conditions (Gouldner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing media content, look for themes and symbols that integrate disparate groups around shared meanings or that reconcile potential conflicts in ways that support social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between ideology and culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture is 'the pattern of meaning embodied in symbolic forms' used for communication (Thompson/Geertz); ideology is meaning tied to interests (class and otherwise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate routine cultural resonance (familiar symbols/themes) from ideological constructions that serve particular group interests when coding content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological level in hierarchical model
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideology is the most macro level in the hierarchy of influences on media content, subsuming extramedia, organizational, routines, and individual levels; processes at lower levels work toward ideologically related message patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analysis, treat ideological influence as overarching context—ask how organizational routines, source choices, and individual practices cumulatively produce messages consistent with broader ideological patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media as agents of social control / boundary maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: A key media function is to maintain cultural boundaries: defining which views and values are within acceptable bounds and which are excluded from legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how stories, placement, tone, and prominence delineate acceptable discourse and marginalize alternatives; track patterns of inclusion/exclusion across issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviance as a criterion for news selection
rubrics_metrics.description: News selection is based on dimensions of deviance (controversial, sensational, prominent, unusual); events covered are often more deviant than those not covered and may convey normative deviance (would violate American norms if they occurred domestically).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating newsworthiness, code for deviance-related attributes (sensationalism, threat to status quo, prominence) as predictors of coverage and prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media techniques for communicating/delegitimizing deviance
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques include trivialization; polarization via counterdemonstrations; emphasis on internal dissension; disparagement by undercounting and minimizing effectiveness; reliance on officials; emphasis on presence of extremists/violence; and attention to opposing forces (Gitlin; McLeod & Hertog).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and catalog these framing techniques (headline choice, photo selection, source emphasis, factual omissions) to diagnose how coverage increases perceived deviance and reduces legitimacy of groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing through selective visuals and headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of photos and headlines can refract meaning (e.g., headline 'Anarchists organize to wreak havoc downtown' or photos emphasizing flag-burning) and thereby misrepresent or delegitimize actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate image/text pairings and headline framing for distortions of event meaning; note what contextual information is omitted that would alter interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hallin's spheres: consensus, legitimate controversy, deviance
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic world divided into sphere of consensus (core values where advocacy is acceptable), sphere of legitimate controversy (region where balance/objectivity is sought), and sphere of deviance (outside mainstream where journalism exposes/condemns/excludes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify issues/actors into these spheres to predict journalistic role (advocate, neutral balancer, or condemner) and to explain differential treatment and boundary enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power as ideology: Marxist paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideology links meaning to relations of domination: meaning is used to establish and sustain asymmetrical power. Media symbolic content systematically furthers interests of certain groups (class, gender, race).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whose interests are served by prevailing representations; attend to patterns that make existing social orders appear natural and inevitable (examination of absent alternatives is crucial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political economy view: ownership and the cultural commodity
rubrics_metrics.description: Media reflect the ideology of owners/funders; ownership is a primary means by which the ruling class exerts control. Media content is a cultural commodity shaped by capitalist drives (e.g., pursuit of lucrative markets, integration of news/business departments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate ownership structures, corporate linkages, and market incentives as explanatory variables for content patterns; look for commodification effects (prioritizing profitable information-gathering over broad public information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variations in ideology by funding source (Altschull's framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four sources of media support: (1) 'official' (state-controlled), (2) 'commercial' (advertiser/media owner ideology), (3) 'interest' (financing group like party/religion), (4) 'informal' (individual contributors). Content reflects the ideology of the paymaster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use funding-source classification to predict ideological slant and to explain cross-national or intra-system variations in media messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental approach / elite integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Media are seen as organically connected to elites (power elite), with media leaders circulating among elite institutions, developing shared values; media actions often serve class interests rather than independent public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map personnel flows, institutional ties (boards, fellowships), and shared organizational networks to demonstrate elite cohesion and its influence on content and norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite news source structure and interlocking sources
rubrics_metrics.description: National media rely on a cohesive, interconnected 'insiders' group of sources (government officials, former officials, journalists, think-tank experts) that span programs and issues; source selections mark the boundaries of political debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply network analysis to sources across programs/issues to reveal interlocking structures; measure source centrality, repetition, and cross-program linkage as indicators of ideological anchoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media restrict debate by framing around government process and centrist experts
rubrics_metrics.description: The media organize debate primarily in relation to the government process and the narrow political range of the two-party system; use of centrist or conservative experts and 'objective' insider journalists anchors conventional wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess guest/expert panels and selection practices for ideological range: count ideological diversity, prevalence of insiders, and tendency to 'balance' within an established comfort zone rather than present radical alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicting elite interventions when stories press ideological boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: From an ideological perspective, elites will intervene against journalistic routines when a story challenges key ideological boundaries (example: intervention by Berkeley president in CBS News's Berkeley Rebels story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In case studies, document instances of elite pushback (funding threats, public complaints, regulatory pressure) as evidence that coverage violated powerful interests' ideological limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media-created extremism / feedback effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Media treatment can create or amplify perceptions of extremism (e.g., marginal groups becoming more shrill when shut out), so 'extremism' is often partly media-produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace feedback loops: examine how coverage choices escalate group behavior and how resulting actions are then covered in ways that confirm initial delegitimizing frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic method: use of network analysis to map source webs
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources are 'linked' when they appear together on the same issue/program; over time this mapping reveals a cohesive central 'insiders' group cutting across issues and programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize linkage rules, construct longitudinal source networks, and use network metrics (cohesion, centralization, overlap) to test hypotheses about elite source dominance and ideological structuring.
